articles.title: Engineering Design Process vs. Scientific Method: What’s the Difference?
articles.excerpt: You pitch a science fair project: build something that actually works. The proposal comes back with one note in red ink. “Where’s your hypothesis?” This happens more than you’d think. On a physics tea…
articles.body: You pitch a science fair project: build something that actually works. The proposal comes back with one note in red ink. “Where’s your hypothesis?” This happens more than you’d think. On a physics teachers’ mailing list, one parent described their daughter wanting to build a guitar amplifier out of transistors. Her teacher shut it down because she couldn’t phrase it as a hypothesis. Elsewhere, a student on the Science Buddies forum got a bad grade on an inclinometer project and was told it was “a demonstration,” not a science project. Building an amplifier is a great project. It just runs on a different process. The scientific method is for answering a question about how the world works. The engineering design process is for building something that solves a problem.
articles.author: Roman Fairchild

articles.title: Spring AI RAG example: index source code with PgVector
articles.excerpt: This Spring AI RAG example builds a source-code index with a Spring AI vector store backed by PgVector. It deduplicates files, splits them into embedding-sized chunks, and returns grounded answers wit…
articles.body: This Spring AI RAG example builds a source-code index with a Spring AI vector store backed by PgVector. It deduplicates files, splits them into embedding-sized chunks, and returns grounded answers with file citations taken from retrieval metadata. Think of it as a local Context7-style index for the library sources your project actually uses, with indexing exposed over MCP. A model trained last year does not know the API you upgraded to last week. By the end, you will have a Spring AI RAG indexer for dependency sources and a chat client that answers from indexed code with file citations. Gradle downloads the source jars, the MCP tool builds the index, and  /api/chat  asks questions against it.

articles.title: Low impact or medium impact? Where NERC CIP impact ratings go wrong
articles.excerpt: The impact rating decides almost everything else in a NERC CIP program: which requirements apply, how much evidence you keep and what an audit looks at. CIP-002-5.1a's bright-line criteria are short,…
articles.body: The impact rating decides almost everything else in a NERC CIP program: which requirements apply, how much evidence you keep and what an audit looks at. CIP-002-5.1a's bright-line criteria are short, but they are easy to misread. These are the mistakes that come up most for generation operators. 1. Rating the sites and forgetting the control room A single solar or wind plant reaches medium impact under criterion 2.1 only at 1,500 MW or more at one plant location in one Interconnection. That threshold is rarely met, so operators conclude the whole program is low impact. Criterion 2.11 is separate: a Control Center or backup Control Center that performs Generator Operator functions for 1,500 MW or more in a single Interconnection is medium impact.

articles.title: chalk and debug shipped malware for a few hours. Waiting 7 days would have skipped it.
articles.excerpt: In September 2025, a maintainer of several very popular npm packages, including chalk and debug, had their account phished. New versions were published with code that tried to steal cryptocurrency fro…
articles.body: In September 2025, a maintainer of several very popular npm packages, including chalk and debug , had their account phished. New versions were published with code that tried to steal cryptocurrency from browsers. The community spotted it quickly, and the bad versions were removed within hours. The teams that got hit were the ones whose installs ran in those hours. Teams that waited even a couple of days never saw the bad versions at all. Most bad releases have a short life Not every bad release is an attack. Most are ordinary mistakes: a broken build published by accident, a regression the tests missed, a missing file.

articles.body: Arc sits frozen under Atlassian. SigmaOS now charges for features Arc gave away. Comet dropped its $200/month paywall and went cross-platform. Once you know where to look, the AI browser market finally has a clear answer. Every few months, someone in my network shares a screenshot of a shiny new browser setup and wonders aloud why everyone isn't using it. There's always a tidier sidebar, a cleverer tab system, or an AI model tucked into the address bar. The replies split just as predictably. Half come from enthusiastic converts. The other half come from people who gave it a try, ran into a wall around their third Chrome extension that refused to work, and quietly went back. The 2025-2026 wave of AI browsers has pushed that debate into serious territory.

articles.title: Total solar eclipse 2027 vs 2028 — Which one should you choose, Egypt or Australia?
articles.excerpt: From six minutes of darkness in Egypt or totality over the Australian Outback, here are the pros and cons of the next two total solar eclipses.
articles.body: For those who want to experience a total solar eclipse, the next two years present the best kind of problem. On Aug. 2, 2027, the so-called "eclipse of the century " will sweep across southern Spain, North Africa and the Middle East, bringing more than six minutes of totality to parts of Egypt. Then, on July 22, 2028, another exceptionally long total solar eclipse will cross Australia, putting the remote Outback and Sydney Harbor in the path of the moon's dark central shadow before it reaches New Zealand's beautiful South Island. Both eclipses will be spectacular, and both will require careful planning, yet they promise very different experiences.

articles.title: NASA's twin ESCAPADE Mars probes slingshot around Earth in unprecedented double 'gravity assist'
articles.excerpt: NASA's twin ESCAPADE spacecraft are wrapping up a year-long voyage to Mars, and are now ready to make a beeline to the Red Planet.
articles.body: Twin NASA spacecraft are wrapping up a year-long escapade, ready to make a beeline to the Red Planet. The Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers (ESCAPADE) spacecraft launched in November 2025 on the second-ever flight of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket. But rather than head straight to Mars, the two spacecraft dawdled through a looping trajectory . Now, they are back in Earth's neighborhood where they tackled a crucial engine burn unusually close to Earth that — if all goes well — will set them on track for Mars . "No NASA mission has ever done this before," said Rob Lillis, a planetary and space physicist at the University of California, Berkeley and principal investigator of the ESCAPADE mission.
